messages.author: 17b683ae7e71acc3
messages.subject: Line Transect analysis
parts:
Hello List.

I am relatively new to the joys of distance, and any comments would be much
appreciated. In 2000 and 2005, around 140 1km squares were surveyed on
Salisbury Plain to look at bird populations in the area. The methods
followed the UK National Breeding Bird Survey, which consists of walking
two one-kilometre lines through each square and recording birds in distance
categories. Each square was visited twice in each year (i.e. 4km walked).
During 2000 the standard categories were used (0-25m 25-100m and 100m+),
however this was increased to 5 in 2005 so that better models could be
fitted to the data (0-10m; 10-25m; 25-100m; 100-250m; 250m+). Each survey
line was split up into five different 200-metre sections and habitats were
recorded on this basis.

The first part of the analysis is to look at density changes between the
two surveys. It is key to investigate changes within the five different
regions of the Plain, as they have received different management. For
this, I only used squares surveyed in both years and confined it to the 0-
25m and 25-100m distance categories. The analysis was undertaken with a
Half Normal model and a Global detection function as this was thought not
to vary across area. For a number of species there was an increase in raw
count data, but a significant decline in density estimate due to large
difference in the models fitted between years. The question is whether
recorder effects should be investigated, or whether it is good enough to
look at an average surveyor in both years. Is there a way of both looking
at Stratum densities (using a Global detection function) while also
investigating recorder effects? Each recorder had the same overall survey
effort, however the same recorder was not always used over both visits to a
square.

Secondly, identifying habitat associations. The survey sample is the
kilometre square, however habitats were recorded on a 200m-section basis
(10 per square). Obviously, these are not independent. Any ideas on how
this should be treated in the analysis.

Regards Andrew Stanbury

messages.author: d718c6bb1db28db2
messages.subject: Re: Line Transect analysis
parts:
Andrew, in principle, you're getting absolute estimates of abundance, and
observer differences won't affect this. You have adjusted for
detectability, which includes any differences in observers. However, the
number of intervals in 2000 was very small (3, effectively 2 for smaller
species), so some bias can be anticipated. Hence you may want to play
around with observer effects. If you use the multiple covariate distance
sampling engine of Distance, you can include observer as a factor type
covariate.

You can classify 200m sections by habitat type, and then estimate density
for each habitat type, by stratifying by habitat type. You'll need to
enter data separately by 200m section and include a field for habitat type
to do this.

Steve Buckland
